passage: In Class 4 at the community school, Ms Swati handed out four coloured cards for the group volcano model: Measurer, Painter, Builder, Reporter. "Each card has a name on the back. On Friday the Reporter tells us who did what." Sabina looked at her Painter card. Usually she let others do the work. Now her name was on the paint, and Ravi, the Reporter, would say so out loud. She mixed red and orange with care. Nobody had to nag. On Friday Ravi said, "Sabina painted the lava." Sabina's cheeks went pink, and she grinned.

qa.q: What did Ravi say about Sabina on Friday?
qa.a: Ravi said, "Sabina painted the lava."

qa.q: How did Sabina feel when hearing Ravi say it on Friday?
qa.a: Sabina felt proud and a little shy, cheeks going pink and grinning; being named made her effort count.

qa.q: What did Ms Swati do that changed how Sabina worked?
qa.a: Ms Swati gave each child a named card and a Reporter to say who did what, so effort became visible without any punishment.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ravi to be the Reporter on Friday?
qa.a: Ravi may have felt important and a bit responsible, holding the job of being fair about who did what in front of the class.

grounding: A teacher assigns each member a named part and a reporter shows who did what, so visible accountability reduces loafing without punishment.

passage: During our garden project Ganga wrote each of our names on a strip of paper with a job, watering, weeding, seed labels, sketching, and stuck the strips on the board. Arohi, who usually disappeared when there was work, read her strip: "seed labels." She grumbled but sat down and wrote nine labels. When the teacher came round, Ganga pointed at the board and said, "You can see who did what." Nobody argued. I could not tell whether Arohi liked her job, but she stayed until the last label was done.

qa.q: How many seed labels did Arohi write?
qa.a: Arohi wrote nine labels.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when sticking the named strips on the board?
qa.a: Ganga was probably hopeful and a little determined that the work would be shared fairly, which shows when Ganga points at the board and says the teacher can see who did what.

qa.q: What choice by Ganga made it hard for anyone to coast?
qa.a: Ganga gave every child a named job on the board, so who did what was visible without anyone being told off.

qa.q: What was it like for Arohi to find her own name next to "seed labels"?
qa.a: Arohi probably felt annoyed and a bit cornered, since she grumbled, yet with her name on the job she sat down and wrote all nine labels.

grounding: A child assigns each member a named part and shows who did what, so visible accountability shrinks loafing without punishment.

passage:
Monday: Group 3's model of the solar system was a mess. Four children, one box of clay, lots of arguing. Vinita sat drawing on her hand while the others shouted.
Wednesday: Bidisha tore a page from her notebook and made a chart. “Sun and Mercury: Bidisha. Venus and Earth: Vinita. Mars and Jupiter: Tarun. Saturn and the rest: Moni. Labels: everyone does their own.” She stuck it on the box. Vinita read her name twice and picked up the blue clay.
Next Monday: At the presentation, each child stood by their planets and explained them. Vinita's Earth had a tiny white North Pole. Ms Dsouza asked who made it. Vinita raised her hand fast.

qa.q: Which planets did the chart give Vinita?
qa.a: Venus and Earth.

qa.q: How did Vinita seem to feel when she read her name twice?
qa.a: She seemed pleased and motivated, as if having her own named part made her want to work.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha's chart work without anyone being told off?
qa.a: It gave each child a named part and showed who did what, so everyone was accountable without punishment.

qa.q: How might Tarun and Moni have felt once the chart went up?
qa.a: They were probably relieved, since the arguing stopped and each knew exactly what to do.

grounding: Shows a child assigning each member a named part and showing who did what, which shrinks coasting without punishment.

passage:
Maria, you're teaching Class 4 now, so let me tell you what I learned when I was about ten myself. I'm your Kavitha aunty, remember.
Our class had to make a village model for Republic Day. Our group was six children, and every day two of them just played with the scissors while four of us worked.
One evening I got angry and wrote on a sheet: “Houses: Kavitha and Leena. Well: Suresh. Trees: Pinto. Fields: Rani. Cows: Jomy.” I pinned it on the model.
The next day, Pinto made fifteen trees. Jomy made cows with little tails. Nobody scolded anyone.
When the headmaster came, each of us showed our own part. Pinto was so proud of his trees he wouldn't stop talking.

qa.q: How many trees did Pinto make?
qa.a: Pinto made fifteen trees.

qa.q: What was young Kavitha feeling when she wrote the sheet?
qa.a: She felt angry and frustrated that two children kept playing while four did the work.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed the group?
qa.a: Pinning up a sheet with each child's named part, which made everyone's work visible so the two who played started working.

qa.q: How might Pinto have felt when the headmaster came?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited, since his trees were clearly his and he could show them off.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a child, assigning each member a named part of a group model, which made everyone accountable without scolding.

passage:
The class newspaper had to be finished in thirty minutes, and the room was noisy with rain drumming on the windows and the fan broken.
Preeti looked at her group of five. Last time, two of them had done nothing. She grabbed a chalk and wrote on the small board: “News: Preeti. Sports: Anil. Weather: Rukhsar. Jokes: Himani. Drawing: Sam.”
Himani, who usually drifted off to look out of the window, stared at the word Jokes. Then she started writing, giggling to herself.
When time was up, each section had a name printed at the bottom. Ms Kapoor read Himani's jokes aloud and the class laughed. Himani went pink with pride.

qa.q: What section did Himani write?
qa.a: Himani wrote the jokes.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when her jokes were read aloud?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy, going pink with pride.

qa.q: Why did Preeti's list work even in a rushed, noisy class?
qa.a: Each person had one clear named section and their name was printed on it, so there was no room to coast.

qa.q: How might Anil and Sam have felt with their names on their sections?
qa.a: They probably felt responsible and a bit proud, knowing everyone could see their part.

grounding: Shows a child giving each member a named section with names printed, which reduces coasting in a rushed setting.

passage:
In Class 5C at a Nagpur school, the last project ended with Pradeep drawing one cloud while Riya did the rest. So this time Hansa ma'am pinned a chart by the board: GROUP 2, SOLAR SYSTEM MODEL. Riya: planets. Pradeep: sun and labels. Mehul: stand. Asha: fact cards.
"Tick your box when your part is done," she said. "On Friday, each of you shows your own part."
Pradeep read his name twice.
On Wednesday he wrote a question mark after PLUTO, because he'd found out it isn't called a planet anymore. By Friday every box had a tick. When his turn came, Pradeep held up the sun and explained why it was so much bigger than the rest.
Riya whispered to Asha, "Finally, I didn't do it all."

qa.q: What was Pradeep's part in the model?
qa.a: Pradeep's part was the sun and labels.

qa.q: What does Pradeep reading his name twice suggest?
qa.a: Pradeep seemed surprised and a little proud to have a job with his name on it, which made the work feel like it mattered.

qa.q: Why did Hansa ma'am's chart work without any punishment?
qa.a: Each child could see their own job and knew they would show it on Friday, so effort was visible and nobody could hide.

qa.q: How is this project different for Riya?
qa.a: Riya feels relieved instead of overloaded, because this time the work is truly shared 😊

grounding: Shows a teacher giving each child a named part and showing who did what, so loafing shrinks without punishment.
